{{nihongo|'''Iibo Nimasu Amaterasu Shrine'''|粒坐天照神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945}} located on Mount Hiyama (Hakuroyama) in {{ill|Tatsuno, Hyōgo|Q877190|qid=Q877190}}, {{ill|Hyōgo Prefecture|Q130290|qid=Q130290}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|fr|Shikinaisha|zh|式內社|qid=Q134917286|lt=Shikinaisha}} ({{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}}) and was ranked as a former {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Prefectural Shrine}} under the {{ill|Q712534|lt=Modern Shrine Ranking System}}. Together with {{ill|Iwa Shrine (Matsumoto)|Q65320|qid=Q65320}} and {{ill|Watatsumi Shrine (Kobe)|Q11559098|qid=Q11559098|lt=Watatsumi Shrine}}, it is collectively known as the “Three Great Shrines of Harima.” The mountain where the shrine stands is said to resemble the shape of a seated dragon, from which its former name, '''Ryūza Shrine''' (“Dragon Seat Shrine”), derives—a name still widely used locally. {{nihongo|'''Iibo Nimasu Amaterasu Shrine'''|粒坐天照神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Harima Province]].

== Enshrined deity ==
{{ill|Amenohoakari|Q10940411|qid=Q10940411|lt=Amateru Kuniteru Hiko Hoakari no Kami}}<ref>“According to tradition, the enshrined deity of this shrine is Amateru Kuniteru Hiko Hoakari no Mikoto. To the west of this shrine, in Isei Village, stands {{ill|Isekisan Shrine|Q17193121|qid=Q17193121}}, whose deity is Amateru Kuniteru Hiko Kushitama Nigihayahi no Mikoto. Although these two deities appear distinct, the {{ill|Kujiki|Q2716751|qid=Q2716751|lt=Kujiki}} identifies Nigihayahi as Hoakari.” (Hyōgo Prefecture Shrine Gazetteer). For a period, Iibonimasu Amaterasu Shrine enshrined Amaterasu Ōmikami as the principal deity in the main hall, and under the influence of State Shinto after the Meiji period, adopted the reading “Amaterasu Shrine.” By contrast, Iseki Sansha Shrine retains the older reading “Amateru Shrine” and distinguishes its deity from Amaterasu Ōmikami. The Kujiki, however, treats Hoakari and Nigihayahi as the same deity.</ref> is enshrined here, and the sacred tree is a {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=cedar}}.

== History ==
The shrine is said to have been founded in the 2nd year of {{ill|Empress Suiko|Q298057|qid=Q298057}} ({{ill|594|Q33625|qid=Q33625}}) at the summit of Mount Hiyama ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hakuroyama}}). Today, the shrine grounds extend from the mountainside down to the foothills. The name “Iibo” (粒) is considered the origin of the place-name “Ibo” (揖保)<ref>However, the claim that Iibonimasu Amaterasu Shrine is the origin of this etymology has only been asserted in relatively recent times; traditionally, {{ill|Nakatomi Itate Shrine|Q17226544|qid=Q17226544}} has been regarded as the stronger candidate.</ref>. During the {{ill|Heian period|Q193292|qid=Q193292}}, the shrine was listed as a {{ill|Myōjin Taisha|Q9610964|qid=Q9610964}} in the {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}<ref>Alternative theories appear in works such as “Jingishi Ryō,” “Harima Kagami,” “Harima Meisho Junran Zue,” and “Ibo-gun Chishi,” which argue for a different location.</ref>.

After the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|Q8707|qid=Q8707}}, Sekiguchi Hisanori, formerly a ceremonial advisor to the {{ill|Tatsuno Domain|fr|Domaine de Tatsuno|ja|龍野藩|ko|다쓰노번|ru|Тацуно (княжество)|zh|龍野藩|qid=Q1012712}}, was appointed priest by order of {{ill|Yasuaya Wakisaka|ja|脇坂安斐|qid=Q11612111}}, then {{ill|domainal governor|ja|知藩事|qid=Q11584647}}, to revive the shrine as the guardian shrine of Tatsuno under {{ill|State Shinto|bn|রাষ্ট্রীয় শিন্তৌ|de|Staats-Shintō|es|Sintoísmo estatal|fa|شینتوی حکومتی|fr|Shintoïsme d'État|id|Shinto Negara|ja|国家神道|ko|국가신토|no|Statsshinto|pt|Xintoísmo estatal|ru|Государственный синтоизм|simple|State Shinto|tr|Devlet Şintoizmi|vi|Thần đạo Quốc gia|zh|国家神道|qid=Q1197248}}. Sekiguchi Kumi, an authority in {{ill|vibration engineering|ja|振動工学|qid=Q11498075}} and former president of {{ill|Himeji Kōgyō Daigaku|ja|姫路工業大学|zh|姬路工業大學|qid=Q11447475}}, was the fourth-generation head of the shrine family and served concurrently as priest. The shrine continues to be maintained by their descendants and related families.

The shrine’s parishioners number about 3,300 households, primarily in Tatsuno-chō on both banks of the {{ill|Ibo River|arz|نهر ايبو|fa|رود ایبو|ja|揖保川|ru|Ибо (река)|qid=Q11498396}}, including areas such as Hiyama, the old castle town of Tatsuno, Kita-Tatsuno, and parts of Isei and Ibogawa.

== Shrine legend ==
During the reigns of the 32nd emperor {{ill|Emperor Sushun|Q349238|qid=Q349238}} and the 33rd {{ill|Empress Suiko|Q298057|qid=Q298057}}, there lived in what is now Tatsuno City a wealthy and virtuous man named Ifukube no Muraji Hakata-hiko. On the first day of the New Year in the 2nd year of Suiko, a strange light appeared above a grove behind his residence. It transformed into a beautiful child who declared himself a messenger of Amateru Kuniteru Hiko Hoakari no Mikoto and bestowed divine instructions and sacred rice seeds. After the seeds were planted, the land prospered, yielding abundant harvests, and the area came to be known as “Iibo,” meaning rice grain. In gratitude, the people enshrined the deity and named the shrine Iibonimasu Amaterasu Shrine, venerating it as their tutelary shrine to this day.
